objectives.statement: Define electrolysis and, for a given cell, label the positive electrode (anode), the negative electrode (cathode) and the electrolyte, stating whether the electrolyte is molten or in aqueous solution.

Trace the two separate charge-carrier paths in a working electrolytic cell: electrons through the external wires and power supply, and ions through the electrolyte, and explain why these two paths never merge into one.

prerequisites.statement: An ionic compound is built from positive and negative ions held together by strong electrostatic attraction in a fixed lattice.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Electrolysis only becomes possible once that lattice is broken down (by melting) or pulled apart (by dissolving), freeing the ions to move; without this idea, 'mobile ion' has no meaning.

prerequisites.statement: A basic series circuit needs a complete loop of conducting material between the two terminals of a power supply before current can flow.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: An electrolytic cell is a circuit with the electrolyte as one 'component' in the loop; without the idea of a complete loop, the role of the electrolyte is easy to miss.

prerequisites.statement: Like charges repel and opposite charges attract.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: This single rule is the entire reason positive ions move to the negative electrode and negative ions move to the positive electrode; it is not a separate fact to memorise per substance.

diagnostic_items.question: Solid sodium chloride does not conduct electricity, but molten sodium chloride does. What has changed between the solid and the liquid?
diagnostic_items.expected_answer: In the solid, the Na+ and Cl- ions are locked in a fixed lattice and cannot move; melting breaks down the lattice so the ions are free to move and carry charge.

common_wrong_answers.answer: Melting turns the ions into atoms, and atoms conduct electricity.
common_wrong_answers.interpretation: The learner assumes conduction requires a change in particle identity, rather than a change in how free the existing ions are to move.

common_wrong_answers.answer: Melting adds free electrons to the sodium chloride, like in a metal.
common_wrong_answers.interpretation: The learner imports the metallic-conduction model (delocalised electrons) into an ionic substance, where the actual carriers are ions, not electrons.

diagnostic_items.interpretation: This checks whether the learner's model of 'ionic lattice' already includes the idea that the ions themselves, not new particles, are the charge carriers once they are freed to move.
diagnostic_items.remediation_action: Ask the learner to draw the solid lattice as a fixed grid of + and - symbols, then redraw the same symbols scattered and free to move after melting; ask what is different about the two drawings (nothing was created or destroyed, only freedom to move).

theory_blocks.title: A bulb that only lights for one of two identical-looking jars
theory_blocks.body:
Picture two jars side by side. One holds solid white sodium chloride crystals; the other holds the same sodium chloride, melted into a colourless liquid at high temperature.

Dip two wires connected to a bulb and a power supply into each jar in turn. The bulb stays dark for the solid jar and lights up for the molten jar, even though both jars contain exactly the same substance, made of exactly the same Na+ and Cl- ions.

Something about the *solid* state itself is blocking the circuit, and something about *melting* fixes it.

The ions are not created, destroyed, or changed into a different particle when the salt melts: a crystal lattice holds every Na+ and Cl- ion locked tightly in place by strong electrostatic attraction to its neighbours, so no ion can travel from one electrode toward the other.

Melting breaks down that fixed lattice (without breaking the ions themselves) and sets the same ions free to drift through the liquid. [[blue:Freely moving charged particles]] are exactly what a current needs, so the bulb lights.

theory_blocks.title: Electrolysis, electrolyte and electrode
theory_blocks.body:
**Electrolysis** is the decomposition (breaking down) of a molten or aqueous ionic compound by passing an electric current through it. The substance being decomposed must already contain ions that are free to move, which is why electrolysis works on a *molten* ionic compound or on an ionic compound *dissolved in water*, but never on the same compound as a rigid solid.

- The **electrolyte** is the molten or dissolved ionic substance that conducts the current, carried by its own ions, and is decomposed in the process.
- An **electrode** is a conducting rod (often an unreactive material such as graphite or platinum) dipped into the electrolyte to connect it to the external circuit.
- The **anode** is the electrode connected to the positive terminal of the power supply, so the anode itself is positive.
- The **cathode** is the electrode connected to the negative terminal of the power supply, so the cathode itself is negative.

Because opposite charges attract, positive ions (cations) in the electrolyte migrate toward the negative cathode, and negative ions (anions) migrate toward the positive anode.

This single attraction rule, not a separate fact for every substance, decides which ions go where.

assets.caption: An electrolytic cell. Inside the electrolyte, positive ions (filled circles marked +) migrate toward the negative cathode and negative ions (filled circles marked -) migrate toward the positive anode; outside the cell, electrons carry the current around the wires and the power supply.
assets.purpose: Shows the two separate charge-carrier paths (ions inside the electrolyte, electrons outside it) and ties electrode polarity to the terminal it is connected to, directly addressing the related idea and the related idea.

theory_blocks.title: Anode and cathode are defined by the connection, not by a fixed sign
theory_blocks.body:
It is tempting to memorise 'anode is positive, cathode is negative' as an arbitrary pair of facts, but both labels follow directly from one rule: [[blue:the electrode is named after the terminal of the supply it is wired to]].

In electrolysis, the supply forces one electrode positive (the anode) and one negative (the cathode) by direct connection; the sign is a *consequence* of the wiring, not an independent property of the word 'anode' itself.

This matters because in a different kind of cell (one that supplies current rather than being driven by an external supply, met in a later topic), the same names can end up on electrodes of the opposite sign.

For electrolysis in this course, always re-derive the polarity from the supply connection rather than relying on memory alone.

theory_blocks.title: Deciding whether a substance will conduct and electrolyse
theory_blocks.body:
Given any substance and its state, ask two questions in order:

1. **Is it ionic?** Electrolysis as described here applies to ionic compounds, molten or in aqueous solution; a covalent substance such as pure liquid hexane has no ions to carry charge and will not conduct this way.
2. **If it is ionic, are the ions free to move?** A solid ionic lattice has ions locked in place (no conduction); the same compound molten, or dissolved in water, has ions free to move (conduction and electrolysis possible).

Only a substance that answers 'yes' to both questions, in this order, will conduct and electrolyse.

theory_blocks.title: Two carriers, two regions, one current
theory_blocks.body:
Look again at the figure above and trace the current all the way around the loop, starting at the negative terminal of the power supply.

Electrons flow out of the negative terminal, through the external wire, to the cathode... and then no further: electrons never enter the electrolyte at all.

Instead, at each electrode a hand-off happens. At the cathode, electrons arriving from the wire are picked up by positive ions arriving from the electrolyte (this hand-off is exactly what 'reduction at the cathode' means, covered in a later lesson).

At the anode, negative ions arriving from the electrolyte give up electrons, which then travel away through the wire to the positive terminal of the supply.

So the current never physically travels as the same particle all the way round: electrons carry it through the metal parts of the circuit, and ions carry it through the electrolyte,

and the two paths only ever meet at the electrode surfaces, never in the middle of the electrolyte.

keywords.definition: The decomposition of a molten or aqueous ionic compound by an electric current.
The molten or dissolved ionic substance that conducts the current and is decomposed.
A conducting rod dipped into the electrolyte to connect it to the external circuit.
The electrode connected to the positive terminal of the supply; it is positive.
The electrode connected to the negative terminal of the supply; it is negative.

worked_examples.statement: **Labelling a cell.** A beaker of molten lead(II) bromide has two graphite rods dipped into it, connected by wires to a power supply. One wire runs from the supply's positive terminal to the left-hand rod; the other runs from the negative terminal to the right-hand rod. Name the left-hand rod, the right-hand rod, and the substance filling the beaker.
solution: The left-hand rod is connected to the positive terminal, so by definition it is the **anode**.
The right-hand rod is connected to the negative terminal, so by definition it is the **cathode**.
The molten lead(II) bromide filling the beaker, which conducts the current and is decomposed, is the **electrolyte**.
worked_examples.interpretation: Naming each part from the supply connection outward, rather than from memory, avoids the common 'anode is always negative' mix-up by construction.

worked_examples.statement: **Which way do the ions go?** The cell above (molten lead(II) bromide, $\mathrm{PbBr_{2}}$) is running. State the direction of migration of the $\mathrm{Pb^{2+}}$ ions and of the $\mathrm{Br^-}$ ions, in terms of anode and cathode.
solution: $\mathrm{Pb^{2+}}$ is a positive ion (cation); positive ions are attracted to the negative electrode, so $\mathrm{Pb^{2+}}$ migrates toward the **cathode**.
$\mathrm{Br^-}$ is a negative ion (anion); negative ions are attracted to the positive electrode, so $\mathrm{Br^-}$ migrates toward the **anode**.
Check: this matches the single attraction rule (opposite charges attract) applied to each ion's own charge, not a separate memorised fact for lead bromide specifically.
worked_examples.interpretation: The same attraction rule, applied twice (once per ion sign), is sufficient; no new rule is needed for a new compound.

worked_examples.statement: **Spot the error.** A student writes: 'In the electrolysis of molten lead bromide, electrons flow from the cathode, through the molten electrolyte, to the anode.' Identify what is wrong with this sentence and rewrite it correctly.
solution: The error is placing electrons *inside* the electrolyte. Electrons are the charge carriers only in the metal wires and the power supply; they do not travel through the molten electrolyte itself.
Inside the electrolyte, the charge carriers are the $\mathrm{Pb^{2+}}$ and $\mathrm{Br^-}$ ions, moving toward the cathode and anode respectively.

Corrected sentence: in the electrolysis of molten lead bromide, electrons flow through the external wires and power supply, while $\mathrm{Pb^{2+}}$ ions migrate through the electrolyte to the cathode and $\mathrm{Br^-}$ ions migrate to the anode.
worked_examples.interpretation: The result follows from the scientific principle used in the solution and shows how to apply that principle when the context or data change.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Treating the whole circuit, electrolyte included, as one continuous electron path.

guided_exercises.statement: A cell has molten potassium chloride, $\mathrm{KCl}$, as the electrolyte, with the left electrode wired to the supply's negative terminal and the right electrode wired to the positive terminal. Label the left and right electrodes, and state the migration direction of the $\mathrm{K^+}$ and $\mathrm{Cl^-}$ ions.
hints: Start from the power supply terminals, not from memory: which terminal is the left electrode wired to?
The electrode wired to the negative terminal is the cathode; the one wired to the positive terminal is the anode.
Positive ions move toward the negative electrode; negative ions move toward the positive electrode.
guided_exercises.answer: The left electrode is the **cathode** (wired to the negative terminal); the right electrode is the **anode** (wired to the positive terminal). $\mathrm{K^+}$ migrates toward the cathode (left); $\mathrm{Cl^-}$ migrates toward the anode (right).
common_errors: Assuming the left electrode must be the anode purely from its position in the diagram, instead of checking which terminal it is actually wired to.

guided_exercises.statement: Explain why a strip of solid copper metal conducts electricity perfectly well, while a lump of solid sodium chloride does not, even though both are solids.
hints: Think about what the charge carriers are in each type of solid.
In a metal, are the carriers free to move even in the solid state?
In an ionic solid, are the ions free to move, or are they held in a fixed lattice?
guided_exercises.answer: Copper is a metal: it has delocalised electrons that are free to move throughout the solid structure at room temperature, so it conducts as a solid. Sodium chloride is ionic: its Na+ and Cl- ions are held in fixed positions in a rigid lattice, with no free-moving charge carriers, so the solid does not conduct; only melting it (or dissolving it) frees the ions to move.
common_errors: Assuming 'solid' always means 'non-conducting', without distinguishing metallic solids (conduct via delocalised electrons) from ionic solids (do not conduct until molten or dissolved).

exercises.statement: A cell has molten calcium chloride, $\mathrm{CaCl_{2}}$, as the electrolyte. Draw and describe the two electrodes and state which ion migrates to which electrode, with a reason.
exercises.answer: Draw two electrodes dipped in the electrolyte, one wired to the supply's positive terminal (the anode) and one to the negative terminal (the cathode). $\mathrm{Ca^{2+}}$, a positive ion, is attracted to the negative cathode and migrates there; $\mathrm{Cl^-}$, a negative ion, is attracted to the positive anode and migrates there.

exercises.statement: A technician claims: 'As soon as I dip the electrodes into any salt, molten or not, the bulb should light.' Using the idea of mobile ions, explain whether the technician is correct.
exercises.answer: The technician is not correct. Whether the bulb lights depends on whether the salt's ions are free to move, not just on the salt being present. If the salt is a rigid solid, its ions are locked in a fixed lattice and cannot carry charge, so the bulb stays off; only once the salt is molten (or dissolved in water) are its ions free to migrate to the electrodes, which is when the bulb lights.
common_errors: Treating 'it is a salt' as sufficient for conduction, without checking the physical state of the ions.

exercises.statement: State, with a reason, whether electrons are present inside the electrolyte of a working electrolytic cell at any point away from the electrode surfaces.
exercises.answer: No. Away from the electrode surfaces, the only charge carriers inside the electrolyte are the electrolyte's own positive and negative ions; electrons are confined to the metal wires, the power supply, and the electrode material itself, never travelling through the body of the molten or aqueous electrolyte.

exercises.statement: A swimming pool's underwater light circuit must never pass current through the pool water deliberately; it is kept entirely separate from the water for safety. Pool water with dissolved salts, however, does conduct electricity to some extent. Using what you have learned about electrolytes and carriers, explain in terms of ions why dissolved (not pure) pool water can conduct, and state what would have to be true of the carriers for pure water with no dissolved ions to conduct in the same way.
exercises.answer: Pool water with dissolved salts contains free-moving dissolved ions (such as $\mathrm{Na^+}$ and $\mathrm{Cl^-}$ from dissolved salts, or other ions from pool treatment chemicals); these mobile ions can carry charge between two points in the water, allowing some conduction, by exactly the same mechanism as any other electrolyte. Pure water, with no dissolved ionic substance, has almost no free ions available as carriers, so it would conduct current only extremely poorly; genuinely significant conduction would require dissolved ions to be present and free to move, not just the water itself.

exam_questions.statement: A student sets up a cell with molten lithium chloride, $\mathrm{LiCl}$, as the electrolyte, two graphite electrodes, and a power supply. (a) State which terminal of the supply the anode must be connected to. (b) State the direction of migration, in terms of anode and cathode, of the $\mathrm{Li^+}$ and $\mathrm{Cl^-}$ ions. (c) Explain why solid lithium chloride could not be used in place of the molten electrolyte.
exam_questions.answer: (a) The anode must be connected to the positive terminal of the supply, since the anode is defined as the electrode wired to the positive terminal. (b) $\mathrm{Li^+}$, a positive ion, migrates toward the cathode; $\mathrm{Cl^-}$, a negative ion, migrates toward the anode, because each ion is attracted to the oppositely charged electrode. (c) In solid lithium chloride, the $\mathrm{Li^+}$ and $\mathrm{Cl^-}$ ions are locked in fixed positions in a rigid ionic lattice; with no ions free to move, no charge can be carried through the solid, so it would not conduct or electrolyse.
mark_scheme: States that the anode is connected to the positive terminal, with the defining link made explicit.
States that $\mathrm{Li^+}$ migrates to the cathode.
States that $\mathrm{Cl^-}$ migrates to the anode.
Explains that the solid's ions are fixed in a lattice and not free to move, so cannot carry charge.

exam_questions.statement: A diagram shows a cell with an arrow drawn through the body of the electrolyte labelled '$e^-$ flows this way'. Explain what is wrong with this labelled arrow, and state, in one sentence each, what actually carries charge in the electrolyte and in the external wires.
exam_questions.answer: The arrow is wrong because electrons never travel through the electrolyte itself; that arrow should instead represent the movement of ions. In the electrolyte, charge is carried by the electrolyte's own positive and negative ions, moving toward the oppositely charged electrodes. In the external wires and power supply, charge is carried by electrons.
mark_scheme: States that electrons do not travel through the electrolyte.
States that ions (positive and negative) carry charge in the electrolyte.
States that electrons carry charge in the external wires/supply.

challenge_questions.statement: A cell contains molten lead(II) bromide, $\mathrm{PbBr_{2}}$, with two identical graphite rods dipped into it, one on the left and one on the right. The left rod is wired to the negative terminal of the supply and the right rod to the positive terminal. While the cell is running, a student disconnects both wires and reconnects them the other way round. Neither rod is moved and the electrolyte is not changed. (a) State which ion now migrates to the left rod and which to the right rod. (b) Explain why the labels 'anode' and 'cathode' have swapped rods even though nothing about the rods themselves has changed. (c) State one thing about this cell that the swap does not change.
hints: Decide first which terminal each rod is now joined to; the names follow from that, not from which side of the beaker the rod sits on.
Then use the attraction rule: which ion is attracted to a rod that is now positive?
challenge_questions.answer: (a) After the swap the left rod is joined to the positive terminal, so $\mathrm{Br^-}$ ions now migrate to it, and the right rod is joined to the negative terminal, so $\mathrm{Pb^{2+}}$ ions now migrate to it: the two migrations have swapped sides. (b) 'Anode' means the electrode connected to the positive terminal and 'cathode' means the electrode connected to the negative terminal; the names describe the connection, not the piece of graphite. Both rods are identical inert graphite, so there is nothing about a rod itself that could make it one or the other, and swapping the wires is enough to swap the names. (c) Several things are unchanged: the electrolyte is still molten lead(II) bromide with the same mobile $\mathrm{Pb^{2+}}$ and $\mathrm{Br^-}$ ions; the rods are still inert graphite; and the rule itself is unchanged, since positive ions still migrate to the negative electrode and negative ions to the positive electrode.
common_errors: Treating 'anode' and 'cathode' as fixed names for the left-hand and right-hand rods, instead of names that follow whichever terminal each rod is connected to.

mcq.stem: In the electrolysis of molten zinc chloride using two graphite electrodes, which statement about the anode is correct?

options.text: The anode is the electrode connected to the positive terminal of the supply, and it is positive.
The anode is always negative, whatever it is connected to.
options.why_wrong: the anode's sign is not a fixed fact; it is positive specifically because it is connected to the positive terminal of the supply.

options.text: The anode is whichever electrode is drawn on the left of the diagram.
options.why_wrong: the position of an electrode in a drawing has no bearing on whether it is the anode; only its connection to the supply does.

options.text: The anode is the electrode where positive ions collect and turn into metal.
options.why_wrong: positive ions are attracted to the negative cathode, where they are discharged, not to the anode.

mcq.explanation: The anode is defined by its connection to the positive terminal of the power supply, which is also why it carries a positive charge; this is a consequence of the wiring, not a separate rule to memorise.

mcq.stem: Which of these best describes what carries charge through a molten electrolyte during electrolysis?

options.text: Electrons, moving from the cathode to the anode.
options.why_wrong: electrons are confined to the external wires and power supply; they do not travel through the electrolyte.

options.text: The electrolyte's own positive and negative ions, each moving toward the oppositely charged electrode.
Neutral atoms, formed as the ions lose their charge mid-way through the electrolyte.
options.why_wrong: ions keep their charge while migrating; they are only discharged once they reach an electrode, not somewhere in the middle of the electrolyte.

options.text: A mixture of electrons and ions moving in the same direction.
options.why_wrong: electrons do not enter the electrolyte at all, and the two types of ion present move in opposite directions, not the same direction.

mcq.explanation: Only the electrolyte's own ions carry charge inside the electrolyte, with cations migrating to the cathode and anions migrating to the anode; electrons are confined to the metallic parts of the circuit.

mcq.stem: Solid potassium bromide does not conduct electricity, but molten potassium bromide does. What is the best explanation?

options.text: Melting changes the $\mathrm{K^+}$ and $\mathrm{Br^-}$ ions into new, more conductive particles.
options.why_wrong: melting does not change what the ions are; it only frees the same ions to move, since no new particles are formed by melting alone.

options.text: Solid potassium bromide has no ions at all, only neutral atoms.
options.why_wrong: potassium bromide is ionic in both the solid and molten states; it is made of $\mathrm{K^+}$ and $\mathrm{Br^-}$ ions throughout, not neutral atoms.

options.text: In the solid, the ions are locked in a fixed lattice; melting frees the same ions to move and carry charge.
Melting adds mobile electrons to the structure, as happens in a metal.
options.why_wrong: potassium bromide remains ionic when molten; its carriers are its own ions, not electrons added from somewhere.

mcq.explanation: The ions are present and charged in both states; only their freedom to move changes between the rigid solid lattice and the molten liquid.

mcq.stem: In a working electrolytic cell, a $\mathrm{Ca^{2+}}$ ion in the electrolyte will migrate toward which electrode, and why?

options.text: The anode, because it is the larger of the two common ions.
options.why_wrong: ion size has nothing to do with which electrode an ion migrates toward; only its charge sign matters.

options.text: Whichever electrode is closer to it at the start.
options.why_wrong: migration direction is set by the ion's charge and the electrode's sign, not by starting distance.

options.text: The anode, because all metal ions are discharged at the anode.
options.why_wrong: metal ions are positive and are attracted to the negative cathode, not the anode.

options.text: The cathode, because it is positively charged and the cathode is negative.

mcq.explanation: $\mathrm{Ca^{2+}}$ is a positive ion, and positive ions are attracted to the oppositely charged electrode, the negative cathode.

flashcards.front: What is electrolysis?
flashcards.back: The decomposition of a molten or aqueous ionic compound by passing an electric current through it.

flashcards.front: How is the anode defined in electrolysis?
flashcards.back: The electrode connected to the positive terminal of the power supply; it is therefore positive.

flashcards.front: Compare the charge carriers inside the electrolyte with the charge carriers in the external wires.
flashcards.back: Inside the electrolyte, charge is carried by the electrolyte's own ions (cations to the cathode, anions to the anode); in the external wires and power supply, charge is carried by electrons.

flashcards.front: Does solid sodium chloride conduct electricity as well as molten sodium chloride?
flashcards.back: No. In the solid, the ions are fixed in a rigid lattice and cannot move; only melting (or dissolving) frees them to carry charge.

flashcards.front: Which ions migrate to the cathode, and which migrate to the anode?
flashcards.back: Positive ions (cations) migrate to the cathode; negative ions (anions) migrate to the anode.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: Electrons flow all the way around the circuit, including straight through the electrolyte, just as they do through a metal wire.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: Learners already have a strong, correct model of current in a metal wire as a flow of electrons, and they extend that single model to every part of a circuit, including the electrolyte, without checking whether the material is a metal.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner describes 'electrons moving through the solution' or draws electron arrows crossing the electrolyte between the two electrodes.
misconceptions.correct_model: Electrons are the charge carriers only in the metal wires and the power supply; inside the electrolyte itself, the charge carriers are the electrolyte's own positive and negative ions, moving in opposite directions toward the oppositely charged electrodes.
misconceptions.remediation: Colour-code a cell diagram: one colour for the electron path (wires and supply only) and a different colour for the ion paths (electrolyte only), and ask the learner to point to exactly where one colour has to stop and the other has to start.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: The anode is always the negative electrode, because 'cathode' sounds positive and 'anode' sounds negative, or because that pattern was memorised from an unrelated context.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: Some learners meet the terms cathode and anode first in the context of a battery supplying current to a circuit (a cell discharging), where the polarity convention is the opposite way round from an electrolytic cell being driven by an external supply; the labels get fixed in memory without the underlying rule.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner labels the electrode connected to the positive terminal of the supply as the cathode, or states 'anode is negative' as a fixed fact rather than deriving it from the connection to the supply.
misconceptions.correct_model: In electrolysis, the anode is defined as the electrode connected to the positive terminal of the supply, so it is positive; the cathode is connected to the negative terminal, so it is negative. The names describe the connection, not a fixed universal sign.
misconceptions.remediation: Always start labelling a new cell diagram from the power supply terminals outward: mark the + and - terminals first, trace the wire to each electrode, and only then write 'anode' on the electrode reached from +.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: A solid ionic salt conducts electricity just as well as the same salt molten, because 'it is still made of charged ions either way'.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: Learners know the ions in a solid ionic compound genuinely carry charge in principle, so they assume charge must therefore be free to move, overlooking that the ions in a solid are locked in fixed lattice positions.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner predicts that a bulb in series with solid sodium chloride will light, or explains solid ionic conduction using the same 'free ion' language used for the molten state.
misconceptions.correct_model: Having charged ions is not enough; the ions must also be free to move from place to place. In a solid ionic lattice, every ion is held in a fixed position by strong attraction to its neighbours, so no net charge can travel through the solid; only melting or dissolving frees the ions to move.
misconceptions.remediation: Test (or describe testing) a bulb in series with solid salt, then with the same salt molten: the bulb stays off for the solid and lights for the melt, with nothing about the ions' charges having changed in between.

common_mistakes.mistake: Drawing or describing electrons travelling through the electrolyte itself.
common_mistakes.why: The electron model of current in metal wires is extended, by habit, to every part of the circuit.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Trace the circuit from the power supply outward and mark exactly where the wire ends and the electrolyte begins; electrons stop there.

common_mistakes.mistake: Stating 'the anode is negative' or 'the cathode is positive' as a fixed, memorised fact.
common_mistakes.why: The terms are sometimes met first in a different context (a cell supplying current) where the polarity convention is reversed.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Always re-derive the sign from the supply connection: anode to positive terminal, cathode to negative terminal.

common_mistakes.mistake: Assuming any ionic solid will conduct electricity just because it is made of charged ions.
common_mistakes.why: Learners focus on the ions having charge and overlook whether those ions are actually free to move.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Ask two separate questions: is it ionic, and are the ions free to move (molten/dissolved, not a rigid solid)?

exam_notes: When asked to label a cell, always work outward from the power supply's + and - terminals, never from memory or from left/right position in a diagram.
When asked why a solid ionic compound does not conduct, state explicitly that the ions are present and charged but are not free to move; do not say the substance 'has no ions'.
Keep the electron path (wires, supply) and the ion paths (electrolyte) as two separate statements in any written answer; marks are often awarded for each path separately.

summary.big_idea: Electrolysis needs ions that are free to move; the electrolyte's ions carry charge to the electrodes while electrons separately carry it through the external circuit.
key_points: A solid ionic lattice has fixed ions and does not conduct; melting or dissolving frees the ions and conduction becomes possible.
The anode is positive because it is wired to the supply's positive terminal; the cathode is negative because it is wired to the negative terminal.
Positive ions (cations) migrate to the cathode; negative ions (anions) migrate to the anode, because opposite charges attract.
Electrons never travel through the electrolyte; they are confined to the wires, the supply, and the electrode surfaces.
summary.what_to_remember_if_nothing_else: Two separate carriers, two separate regions: ions move through the electrolyte, electrons move through the external circuit, and the two paths only meet at the electrode surfaces.

exit_check.question: A cell has molten magnesium bromide, $\mathrm{MgBr_{2}}$, as its electrolyte. State which ion migrates to which electrode, and name the actual charge carrier inside the wires connecting the electrodes to the supply.
exit_check.answer: $\mathrm{Mg^{2+}}$, a positive ion, migrates to the cathode; $\mathrm{Br^-}$, a negative ion, migrates to the anode. Inside the external wires, the charge carrier is electrons, not ions.

objectives.statement: Name the products formed, and the observations that reveal them, at each electrode for molten lead(II) bromide, concentrated aqueous sodium chloride and dilute sulfuric acid, using inert electrodes.

State the general pattern for electrolysing a molten binary ionic compound (metal at the cathode, non-metal at the anode) and use it to predict the products for a molten binary compound not met before.

prerequisites.statement: an earlier lesson: in an electrolytic cell, positive ions (cations) migrate to the cathode and negative ions (anions) migrate to the anode, carried by the electrolyte's own ions.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Predicting a product starts from knowing which ion has already arrived at which electrode; without that, 'discharge' has nothing to act on.

prerequisites.statement: C02: ions and ionic bonds, including how to read the charge on a simple ion from its formula (e.g. Pb2+, Br-, Na+, H+).
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Deciding which ion is reduced or oxidised, and balancing the resulting half-equation, requires knowing each ion's charge.

diagnostic_items.question: Solid sodium chloride, NaCl, is dissolved in water. Name the two ions that the sodium chloride itself puts into the solution, and give the charge on each.
diagnostic_items.expected_answer: Sodium ions, Na+, each carrying a charge of 1+, and chloride ions, Cl-, each carrying a charge of 1-. Dissolving breaks up the lattice, so these ions are free to move through the solution.

common_wrong_answers.answer: NaCl molecules, which are neutral and have no charge.
common_wrong_answers.interpretation: The learner is treating an ionic compound as though it were made of neutral molecules, so nothing in the solution has a charge for an electrode to attract.
The learner has the charges the wrong way round: the metal loses electrons and becomes positive, the non-metal gains them and becomes negative.

diagnostic_items.interpretation: This checks that the learner can read each ion and its charge straight from the formula. Every prediction in this lesson starts by asking which positive ions and which negative ions are present, so a learner who cannot name them cannot begin.
diagnostic_items.remediation_action: Ask the learner to write the group number of each element (sodium in Group I, chlorine in Group VII), then say which one loses an electron and which gains one, and check that 1+ and 1- cancel to give the neutral formula NaCl. Repeat with MgCl2 to show why two chloride ions are needed.

theory_blocks.title: The simplest case first: only two ions to choose from
theory_blocks.body:
Molten lead(II) bromide, $\mathrm{PbBr_{2}}$, is the cleanest possible electrolysis to reason about, because exactly two types of ion are present and nothing else: $\mathrm{Pb^{2+}}$ and $\mathrm{Br^-}$.

There is no competition, no third candidate ion, and no water. $\mathrm{Pb^{2+}}$ migrates to the cathode (opposite charges attract) and is [[blue:**discharged**]] there,

meaning it gains electrons and turns into neutral lead atoms, which collect as a silvery liquid bead. $\mathrm{Br^-}$ migrates to the anode and is discharged there,

losing electrons and turning into bromine molecules, $\mathrm{Br_{2}}$, seen as orange-brown fumes.

Every other case in this lesson is harder only because more candidate ions are available; the underlying idea, that whichever ion actually arrives and is discharged at an electrode decides the product there, never changes.

theory_blocks.title: Observations are the evidence, not the explanation
Adding water changes the list of candidates
theory_blocks.body:
Now dissolve an ionic compound in water instead of melting it. Water itself, $\mathrm{H_{2}O}$, very slightly provides two extra candidate ions everywhere in the solution: $\mathrm{H^+}$ (a possible cathode candidate, alongside the solute's metal ion) and $\mathrm{OH^-}$ (a possible anode candidate, alongside the solute's negative ion, where one is present).

An aqueous electrolyte therefore usually has two candidates competing at each electrode (dilute sulfuric acid, whose only cation is $\mathrm{H^+}$ itself, is an exception at the cathode), where a molten electrolyte of the same compound would have had only one.

This single difference, water present or not, is the entire reason the aqueous and molten cases need separate rules, and why the same compound can give different products depending on its state.

theory_blocks.title: Core aqueous rules: cathode and anode
theory_blocks.body:
**At the cathode** (choosing between the solute's metal ion and $\mathrm{H^+}$ from water): if the metal is more reactive than hydrogen (true for all the common reactive metals met so far, such as sodium, potassium, calcium, magnesium, zinc and iron), $\mathrm{H^+}$ is discharged instead of the metal ion, so **hydrogen gas** forms at the cathode. Only a metal less reactive than hydrogen (such as copper) would itself be deposited at the cathode from aqueous solution.

**At the anode** (choosing between a halide ion, if present, and $\mathrm{OH^-}$/water): a concentrated halide ion, such as $\mathrm{Cl^-}$ in concentrated sodium chloride solution, is discharged in preference to water, producing the halogen gas, here **chlorine**. Where no halide ion is present, as in dilute sulfuric acid, water itself is oxidised at the anode, producing **oxygen gas**.

Applying both rules: concentrated $\mathrm{NaCl(aq)}$ gives hydrogen at the cathode and chlorine at the anode;

dilute $\mathrm{H_{2}SO_{4}(aq)}$ gives hydrogen at the cathode (its only cation is $\mathrm{H^+}$ itself) and oxygen at the anode (it has no halide ion to compete with water).

assets.caption: Three cells compared side by side, each showing the cathode product on the left and the anode product on the right. The cathode product changes from a metal (molten case) to hydrogen (both aqueous cases); the anode product changes from a non-metal (molten), to a halogen (concentrated halide present), to oxygen (no halide present).
assets.purpose: A direct side-by-side comparison that shows 'aqueous' is not one fixed rule, addressing DISC-C04-01 and the related idea together.

theory_blocks.title: Hydrogen's electrode is decided by its charge, not by being a gas
theory_blocks.body:
Dilute sulfuric acid produces a gas at both electrodes, which tempts a guess that either gas could go at either electrode.

It cannot: $\mathrm{H^+}$ is positively charged, so by the same attraction rule used throughout this unit it can only migrate to [[blue:the negative cathode]], never [[red:the anode]], whatever physical state the resulting product happens to have.

Decide the electrode from the ion's charge first; only afterwards ask what the resulting product looks like.

theory_blocks.title: The observations to quote at each electrode
theory_blocks.body:
Two of the three Core electrolytes give a colourless gas at an electrode, so 'bubbles of gas' on its own never identifies a product; the test does.

These are the observations to quote for the three electrolytes named in the syllabus, all with inert (platinum or carbon/graphite) electrodes:

| Electrolyte | At the cathode | At the anode |
|---|---|---|
| molten $\mathrm{PbBr_{2}}$ | a shiny, silvery bead of molten lead collects on the electrode | orange-brown fumes of bromine |
| concentrated $\mathrm{NaCl(aq)}$ | bubbles of a colourless gas: hydrogen, which gives a squeaky pop with a lighted splint | bubbles of a pale yellow-green gas with a sharp, choking smell: chlorine, which bleaches damp litmus paper |
| dilute $\mathrm{H_{2}SO_{4}(aq)}$ | bubbles of a colourless gas: hydrogen, squeaky pop with a lighted splint | bubbles of a colourless gas: oxygen, which relights a glowing splint |

One further observation for dilute sulfuric acid: gas collects about [[blue:twice as fast at the cathode as at the anode]], because $\mathrm{2H_{2}O \rightarrow 2H_{2} + O_{2}}$ makes two molecules of hydrogen for every one molecule of oxygen.

A full answer therefore has two halves at each electrode: what is seen (the colour, state or smell, or bubbles), and the test result that pins the identity down.

theory_blocks.title: Discharge and the half-equations for molten lead(II) bromide
theory_blocks.body:
**Discharge** is the process by which an ion that reaches an electrode loses its charge and becomes a neutral atom or molecule, by gaining or losing electrons.

At the cathode (reduction, electrons gained): $$\mathrm{Pb^{2+} + 2e^- \rightarrow Pb}$$

At the anode (oxidation, electrons lost): $$\mathrm{2Br^- \rightarrow Br_{2} + 2e^-}$$

Both half-equations balance: charge on the left of the cathode equation is $(+2) + (-2) = 0$, matching the 0 charge of neutral $\mathrm{Pb}$ on the right;

charge on the left of the anode equation is $(-2)$, matching $0 + (-2) = -2$ on the right. The two half-equations also use the same number of electrons (2),

so they combine directly into the overall equation $\mathrm{Pb^{2+} + 2Br^- \rightarrow Pb + Br_{2}}$.

assets.caption: Electrolysis of molten lead(II) bromide, heated in a crucible until it melts. $\mathrm{Pb^{2+}}$ migrates to the cathode and is reduced to liquid lead; $\mathrm{Br^-}$ migrates to the anode and is oxidised to orange-brown bromine. No water is present, so these are the only two ions available.
assets.purpose: Ties the discharge idea to a labelled apparatus diagram with explicit ion-migration arrows, and pre-empts the related idea by stating 'no water present' directly on the diagram.

theory_blocks.title: Going further: the general pattern for a molten binary compound
theory_blocks.body:
For *any* molten binary ionic compound (made of just one metal and one non-metal, with no water present), the same two-ion logic as lead(II) bromide always applies,

because a molten binary compound never has more than its own two ions to choose from: **the metal forms at the cathode, and the non-metal forms at the anode.** For example,

molten zinc chloride, $\mathrm{ZnCl_{2}}$, gives zinc metal at the cathode ($\mathrm{Zn^{2+} + 2e^- \rightarrow Zn}$) and chlorine gas at the anode ($\mathrm{2Cl^- \rightarrow Cl_{2} + 2e^-}$),

by exactly the same reasoning as lead(II) bromide, with no new rule needed.

This pattern is specifically for the *molten* state. The moment water is added, the Core aqueous rules above take over instead, because water supplies the extra competing candidates that a molten compound never has.

keywords.definition: The process by which an ion reaching an electrode loses its charge and becomes a neutral atom or molecule.
An electrode, such as graphite or platinum, that conducts current without itself reacting or dissolving.
A liquefied ionic compound made of just one metal and one non-metal, with no water present.
When more than one ion could be discharged at an electrode, the one actually discharged, decided by reactivity (cathode) or concentration (anode).
A solution containing a relatively large amount of dissolved solute per unit volume, which here determines whether a halide ion out-competes water at the anode.

worked_examples.statement: **Molten lead(II) bromide.** State the product formed at each electrode when molten $\mathrm{PbBr_{2}}$ is electrolysed using inert electrodes, and give one observation for each.
solution: Only $\mathrm{Pb^{2+}}$ and $\mathrm{Br^-}$ ions are present (no water in a molten compound).
$\mathrm{Pb^{2+}}$ migrates to the cathode and is discharged: $\mathrm{Pb^{2+} + 2e^- \rightarrow Pb}$. Observation: a silvery liquid bead of lead collects at the cathode.
$\mathrm{Br^-}$ migrates to the anode and is discharged: $\mathrm{2Br^- \rightarrow Br_{2} + 2e^-}$. Observation: orange-brown bromine fumes are seen at the anode.
worked_examples.interpretation: With only two ions present, the discharge logic applies directly, with no competition to resolve.

worked_examples.statement: **Concentrated sodium chloride solution.** State the product formed at each electrode when concentrated $\mathrm{NaCl(aq)}$ is electrolysed using inert electrodes, and explain why the metal, sodium, is not produced.
solution: Candidates at the cathode: $\mathrm{Na^+}$ (from the solute) and $\mathrm{H^+}$ (from water). Sodium is more reactive than hydrogen, so $\mathrm{H^+}$ is discharged instead: hydrogen gas forms at the cathode, tested with a lit splint giving a squeaky pop.

Candidates at the anode: $\mathrm{Cl^-}$ (from the solute) and $\mathrm{OH^-}$/water. The solution is concentrated in chloride ions, so $\mathrm{Cl^-}$ is discharged in preference to water: chlorine gas forms at the anode, identified by its pale green colour and its bleaching effect on damp litmus paper.

Sodium is not produced because $\mathrm{Na^+}$ loses the competition at the cathode to $\mathrm{H^+}$; a metal only appears at the cathode from aqueous solution when it is less reactive than hydrogen, which sodium is not.
worked_examples.interpretation: The result follows from the scientific principle used in the solution and shows how to apply that principle when the context or data change.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Predicting sodium metal at the cathode simply because sodium chloride is the compound named.

worked_examples.statement: **Why does dilute sulfuric acid not behave like concentrated sodium chloride solution?** Both are aqueous electrolytes electrolysed with inert electrodes, yet one produces chlorine at the anode and the other produces oxygen. Explain the difference.
solution: At the cathode, both solutions behave the same way for the same reason: hydrogen ions are discharged in preference to any other cation present, whether that is $\mathrm{Na^+}$ (too reactive to be discharged ahead of hydrogen) in sodium chloride solution, or the acid's own $\mathrm{H^+}$ directly in sulfuric acid, so both cells produce hydrogen gas at the cathode.

The difference is entirely at the anode. Concentrated sodium chloride solution has a high concentration of $\mathrm{Cl^-}$ ions available, which are discharged in preference to water, giving chlorine.

Dilute sulfuric acid, $\mathrm{H_{2}SO_{4}}$, contains sulfate ions, $\mathrm{SO_{4}^{2-}}$, not a halide ion at all, so there is no halide to compete with water at the anode; water itself is oxidised instead, giving oxygen.
Check: the anode product depends on *which anion is actually present and how concentrated it is*, not on the solution simply being aqueous or being an acid.
worked_examples.interpretation: Comparing two aqueous cases side by side isolates exactly which variable (the anion present) controls the anode product, rather than treating 'aqueous' as a single fixed rule.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Assuming every aqueous electrolysis must give the same pair of gases as sodium chloride solution.

worked_examples.statement: **A new molten binary compound.** Molten potassium iodide, $\mathrm{KI}$, is electrolysed with inert electrodes. Predict the product at each electrode, with a half-equation for each.
solution: $\mathrm{KI}$ is a molten binary ionic compound, so the general pattern applies: metal at the cathode, non-metal at the anode, with only $\mathrm{K^+}$ and $\mathrm{I^-}$ present (no water).
Cathode: $\mathrm{K^+ + e^- \rightarrow K}$, giving potassium metal.
Anode: $\mathrm{2I^- \rightarrow I_{2} + 2e^-}$, giving iodine (seen as a purple vapour/dark solid condensing on cooling).
worked_examples.interpretation: Transfers the general molten-binary pattern established with lead(II) bromide to a compound not previously named, checking the rule generalises rather than being memorised for one example only.

guided_exercises.statement: Molten magnesium chloride, $\mathrm{MgCl_{2}}$, is electrolysed with inert electrodes. Name the product at each electrode and give a half-equation for each.
hints: List the ions actually present in molten $\mathrm{MgCl_{2}}$: is water involved at all?
Apply the molten-binary pattern: which ion goes to the cathode, and what does it become?
Balance each half-equation by checking that the charge is the same on both sides.
guided_exercises.answer: Only $\mathrm{Mg^{2+}}$ and $\mathrm{Cl^-}$ are present (no water in a molten compound). Cathode: $\mathrm{Mg^{2+} + 2e^- \rightarrow Mg}$, giving magnesium metal. Anode: $\mathrm{2Cl^- \rightarrow Cl_{2} + 2e^-}$, giving chlorine gas.
common_errors: Mentioning hydrogen or oxygen from water, forgetting that a molten compound has no water present at all.

guided_exercises.statement: Concentrated hydrochloric acid, $\mathrm{HCl(aq)}$, is electrolysed with inert electrodes. Predict the product at each electrode, explaining your reasoning for the anode in particular.
hints: At the cathode, what are the two candidate cations, and which one wins for an acid with no metal present?
At the anode, is a halide ion present here (unlike in dilute sulfuric acid), and is it concentrated?
Compare this case directly to concentrated sodium chloride solution for the anode decision.
guided_exercises.answer: Cathode: the only cation present is $\mathrm{H^+}$ (there is no metal ion), so hydrogen gas forms: $\mathrm{2H^+ + 2e^- \rightarrow H_{2}}$. Anode: unlike dilute sulfuric acid, hydrochloric acid does contain a halide ion, $\mathrm{Cl^-}$; because the acid is concentrated, chloride is discharged in preference to water, giving chlorine gas: $\mathrm{2Cl^- \rightarrow Cl_{2} + 2e^-}$.
common_errors: Assuming every acid must behave exactly like dilute sulfuric acid, without checking whether a halide ion is present and concentrated.

exercises.statement: State the products, with observations, at the cathode and anode for the electrolysis of dilute sulfuric acid, $\mathrm{H_{2}SO_{4}(aq)}$, using inert electrodes.
exercises.answer: Cathode: hydrogen gas, $\mathrm{2H^+ + 2e^- \rightarrow H_{2}}$, identified by a lit splint producing a squeaky pop. Anode: oxygen gas, from the oxidation of water (no halide ion is present to compete), identified by a glowing splint relighting.

exercises.statement: A student electrolyses concentrated aqueous sodium chloride and collects a gas at each electrode. The gas from the anode turns damp blue litmus paper white (bleaches it). Identify this gas and explain, in terms of ion discharge, why it forms at the anode rather than the cathode.
exercises.answer: The gas is chlorine, $\mathrm{Cl_{2}}$. It forms at the anode because $\mathrm{Cl^-}$ is a negative ion, so it migrates to the positive anode; being present at high (concentrated) concentration, it is discharged there in preference to water, losing electrons to form $\mathrm{Cl_{2}}$: $\mathrm{2Cl^- \rightarrow Cl_{2} + 2e^-}$.

exercises.statement: Molten zinc bromide, $\mathrm{ZnBr_{2}}$, is electrolysed with inert electrodes. Predict the product at each electrode, with a half-equation for each, and check that both half-equations balance by charge.
exercises.answer: Cathode: $\mathrm{Zn^{2+} + 2e^- \rightarrow Zn}$ (charge: $+2 + (-2) = 0$, matching neutral Zn), giving zinc metal. Anode: $\mathrm{2Br^- \rightarrow Br_{2} + 2e^-}$ (charge: $2 \times (-1) = -2$, matching $0 + (-2) = -2$ on the right), giving bromine.

exercises.statement: A factory electrolyses molten aluminium oxide, $\mathrm{Al_{2}O_{3}}$, to extract aluminium metal, and separately electrolyses concentrated brine (aqueous sodium chloride) to produce chlorine gas for water treatment. A new trainee says: 'Both processes decompose a compound made of a metal and a non-metal, so they must follow exactly the same rule for predicting products.' Using the ideas from this lesson, explain why the trainee is only partly right, identifying the one factor that makes the two processes follow different rules.
exercises.answer: The trainee is right that both compounds are made of a metal combined with a non-metal, but that alone is not what decides the product-prediction rule; whether water is present is what decides it. Molten aluminium oxide has no water present, so the molten-binary pattern applies directly: aluminium (the metal) forms at the cathode and oxygen (the non-metal, from the oxide ion) forms at the anode, with no competition. Concentrated brine is aqueous, so water supplies competing $\mathrm{H^+}$ and $\mathrm{OH^-}$ ions at each electrode: at the cathode $\mathrm{H^+}$ outcompetes the reactive metal $\mathrm{Na^+}$, giving hydrogen rather than sodium, and only at the anode does the solute's own ion, $\mathrm{Cl^-}$, win (because it is concentrated), giving chlorine. The one factor that changes the applicable rule is the presence of water, not simply 'metal plus non-metal'.

exam_questions.statement: Molten lead(II) bromide and dilute sulfuric acid are each electrolysed with inert electrodes. (a) Name the product at each electrode for molten lead(II) bromide, with a half-equation for each. (b) Name the product at each electrode for dilute sulfuric acid. (c) State the one difference between the two electrolytes that explains why hydrogen and oxygen are produced in one case but not the other.
exam_questions.answer: (a) Cathode: lead, $\mathrm{Pb^{2+} + 2e^- \rightarrow Pb}$. Anode: bromine, $\mathrm{2Br^- \rightarrow Br_{2} + 2e^-}$. (b) Cathode: hydrogen gas. Anode: oxygen gas. (c) Dilute sulfuric acid is aqueous, so water is present: $\mathrm{H^+}$ ions in the solution are reduced to hydrogen and water is oxidised to oxygen; molten lead(II) bromide contains no water at all, only $\mathrm{Pb^{2+}}$ and $\mathrm{Br^-}$, so neither hydrogen nor oxygen can form there.
mark_scheme: States lead at the cathode with a correctly balanced half-equation.
States bromine at the anode with a correctly balanced half-equation.
States hydrogen at the cathode and oxygen at the anode for dilute sulfuric acid.
Identifies the presence or absence of water as the explaining factor.
Explicitly links 'no water in the molten compound' to 'no hydrogen or oxygen can form'.

exam_questions.statement: Concentrated aqueous sodium chloride is electrolysed with inert electrodes. A student predicts: 'Sodium metal will form at the cathode, because sodium chloride contains sodium ions.' (a) State whether the student is correct. (b) Identify the actual cathode product. (c) Explain, by naming both candidate cations and comparing their reactivity, why your answer to (b) is correct.
exam_questions.answer: (a) The student is not correct. (b) The actual cathode product is hydrogen gas. (c) The two candidate cations present at the cathode are $\mathrm{Na^+}$ (from the dissolved sodium chloride) and $\mathrm{H^+}$ (from the water). Sodium is more reactive than hydrogen, and for any metal more reactive than hydrogen, $\mathrm{H^+}$ is discharged in preference to the metal ion; so hydrogen gas forms at the cathode instead of sodium metal.
mark_scheme: States that the student is incorrect.
States hydrogen gas as the actual cathode product.
Names both candidate cations, $\mathrm{Na^+}$ and $\mathrm{H^+}$.
Explains the outcome using sodium's reactivity relative to hydrogen.

exam_questions.statement: Concentrated aqueous sodium chloride is electrolysed using inert carbon electrodes. (a) Describe what is seen at the cathode and name the gas formed there. (b) Describe what is seen and smelt at the anode and name the gas formed there. (c) Give one test, with its result, that would confirm the identity of the gas formed at the anode.
exam_questions.answer: (a) Bubbles of a colourless gas (effervescence) are seen at the cathode; the gas is hydrogen. (b) Bubbles of a pale yellow-green gas are seen at the anode, and the gas has a sharp, choking smell; the gas is chlorine. (c) Holding damp blue litmus paper in the gas at the anode bleaches it white (it may turn red first), confirming chlorine.
mark_scheme: Describes bubbles of a colourless gas (effervescence) at the cathode.
Names the cathode gas as hydrogen.
Describes the anode gas as pale yellow-green (or green) in colour.
Names the anode gas as chlorine, or describes its sharp choking smell.
Gives a valid test with its result: damp litmus paper is bleached white.

challenge_questions.statement: Concentrated aqueous copper(II) chloride, $\mathrm{CuCl_{2}(aq)}$, is electrolysed with inert (graphite) electrodes. Using both the cathode rule and the anode rule from this lesson, predict the product at each electrode, and explain why this case is different from both concentrated sodium chloride solution and dilute sulfuric acid.
hints: At the cathode, compare copper's reactivity to hydrogen's, not sodium's.
At the anode, check whether a halide ion is present and concentrated, as in the brine case.
challenge_questions.answer: Cathode: copper is less reactive than hydrogen, so (unlike sodium) $\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}$ wins the competition against $\mathrm{H^+}$ and is discharged: $\mathrm{Cu^{2+} + 2e^- \rightarrow Cu}$, depositing copper metal. Anode: chloride ions are present at high concentration, so (exactly as in brine) $\mathrm{Cl^-}$ is discharged in preference to water: $\mathrm{2Cl^- \rightarrow Cl_{2} + 2e^-}$, giving chlorine gas. This case differs from concentrated $\mathrm{NaCl(aq)}$ because the cathode rule gives a different winner (copper, not hydrogen, since copper is less reactive than hydrogen while sodium is more reactive), and it differs from dilute $\mathrm{H_{2}SO_{4}(aq)}$ because a concentrated halide ion is present here to win at the anode, whereas sulfuric acid has no halide ion at all.
common_errors: Applying the sodium-chloride cathode result (hydrogen forms) without checking that copper, unlike sodium, is less reactive than hydrogen.

mcq.stem: Concentrated aqueous sodium chloride is electrolysed with inert electrodes. What forms at the cathode, and why?

options.text: Hydrogen gas, because $\mathrm{H^+}$ from water is discharged in preference to the more reactive metal's ion.
Sodium metal, because sodium chloride supplies $\mathrm{Na^+}$ ions.
options.why_wrong: sodium is more reactive than hydrogen, so $\mathrm{H^+}$ from water is discharged instead of $\mathrm{Na^+}$.

options.text: Chlorine gas, because chlorine is the element named in the compound.
options.why_wrong: chlorine forms from $\mathrm{Cl^-}$ at the anode, not the cathode; the compound's name does not decide which electrode a product appears at.

options.text: Sodium hydroxide, formed directly at the cathode.
options.why_wrong: sodium hydroxide is a product remaining in solution after electrolysis, not a substance discharged at the cathode itself.

mcq.explanation: Sodium is more reactive than hydrogen, so $\mathrm{H^+}$ from water wins the competition at the cathode, producing hydrogen gas instead of sodium metal.

mcq.stem: Which statement correctly explains why molten lead(II) bromide produces no hydrogen or oxygen gas?

options.text: Lead is less reactive than hydrogen, so $\mathrm{Pb^{2+}}$ wins the competition against $\mathrm{H^+}$ at the cathode.
options.why_wrong: there is no $\mathrm{H^+}$ to compete with: a molten compound contains no water, so no competition happens at all (and this would not explain the absence of oxygen at the anode either).

options.text: No water is present in the molten compound, so there is no source of $\mathrm{H^+}$ or $\mathrm{OH^-}$ to be discharged.
The electrodes used are inert, so no hydrogen or oxygen can form regardless of the electrolyte.
options.why_wrong: inert electrodes only mean the electrode material itself is not involved in the reaction; whether hydrogen or oxygen can form depends on whether water is present in the electrolyte, not on the electrode material.

options.text: Hydrogen and oxygen only ever form at the anode, and both ions in this compound happen to be cations.
options.why_wrong: $\mathrm{Br^-}$ is an anion, not a cation, and hydrogen forms at the cathode, not the anode.

mcq.explanation: A molten ionic compound contains only its own ions; without water present there is no $\mathrm{H^+}$ or $\mathrm{OH^-}$ available to be discharged at either electrode.

mcq.stem: Dilute sulfuric acid is electrolysed with inert electrodes, producing a gas at each electrode. At which electrode does hydrogen gas form, and why?

options.text: The anode, because hydrogen is a gas and gases are produced at the anode.
options.why_wrong: the electrode a gas forms at depends on the charge of the ion discharged, not on the product simply being a gas; in this unit gases form at both electrodes (hydrogen at the cathode; chlorine or oxygen at the anode).

options.text: The anode, because sulfuric acid is an acid and acids react at the anode.
options.why_wrong: being an acid is not what decides the electrode; the charge on the ion being discharged is what decides it, and $\mathrm{H^+}$ is positive.

options.text: The cathode, because $\mathrm{H^+}$ is a positive ion and migrates to the negative cathode.
Either electrode, depending on the concentration of the acid.
options.why_wrong: the electrode for a given ion is fixed by its charge sign, not by concentration; concentration can affect which ion wins a competition at one electrode, not which electrode an ion migrates to.

mcq.explanation: $\mathrm{H^+}$ is positively charged, so like every cation in this unit it migrates to the negative cathode and is discharged there as hydrogen gas.

mcq.stem: Molten potassium bromide, $\mathrm{KBr}$, is electrolysed with inert electrodes. Which pair of products, at cathode and anode respectively, is correct?

options.text: Hydrogen at the cathode, oxygen at the anode.
options.why_wrong: this would require water to be present; molten potassium bromide contains no water, so no hydrogen or oxygen can form.

options.text: Bromine at the cathode, potassium at the anode.
options.why_wrong: the electrodes are swapped: $\mathrm{K^+}$ is positive and must go to the cathode, while $\mathrm{Br^-}$ is negative and must go to the anode, not the reverse.

options.text: Potassium bromide reforms unchanged at both electrodes.
options.why_wrong: electrolysis decomposes the compound into its elements; the original compound does not simply reform at the electrodes.

options.text: Potassium at the cathode, bromine at the anode.

mcq.explanation: Molten potassium bromide has only $\mathrm{K^+}$ and $\mathrm{Br^-}$ present, so by the molten-binary pattern the metal, potassium, forms at the cathode and the non-metal, bromine, forms at the anode.

flashcards.front: What does 'discharge' mean for an ion at an electrode?
flashcards.back: The ion reaching the electrode loses its charge and becomes a neutral atom or molecule, by gaining or losing electrons.

flashcards.front: When does a metal, rather than hydrogen, form at the cathode in an aqueous electrolysis?
flashcards.back: Only when the metal is less reactive than hydrogen (such as copper); for a more reactive metal, $\mathrm{H^+}$ from water is discharged instead.

flashcards.front: Compare the ions available in molten lead(II) bromide with the ions available in concentrated aqueous sodium chloride.
flashcards.back: Molten $\mathrm{PbBr_{2}}$ has only $\mathrm{Pb^{2+}}$ and $\mathrm{Br^-}$ (no water); concentrated $\mathrm{NaCl(aq)}$ additionally has $\mathrm{H^+}$ and $\mathrm{OH^-}$ from water, competing with $\mathrm{Na^+}$ and $\mathrm{Cl^-}$ respectively.

flashcards.front: Does hydrogen gas form at the anode because it is a gas?
flashcards.back: No. The electrode depends only on the ion's charge; $\mathrm{H^+}$ is a positive ion, so hydrogen always forms at the cathode, whatever state the product is in.

flashcards.front: Dilute sulfuric acid gives hydrogen and oxygen at the electrodes, but concentrated sodium chloride solution gives hydrogen and chlorine. Why the difference at the anode?
flashcards.back: Sulfuric acid has no halide ion, so water is oxidised to oxygen; sodium chloride solution has a concentrated halide ion, $\mathrm{Cl^-}$, which is discharged instead, giving chlorine.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: Electrolysing any aqueous solution always produces the dissolved solute's metal at the cathode, because 'that is the metal ion that is there'.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: In the molten case, the only cation present is the compound's own metal ion, so learners correctly see the metal forming at the cathode; they then carry that single-cation reasoning over to the aqueous case without noticing that water itself supplies a second, competing cation, $\mathrm{H^+}$.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner predicts sodium metal at the cathode when electrolysing concentrated aqueous sodium chloride, instead of hydrogen gas.
misconceptions.correct_model: An aqueous solution always contains $\mathrm{H^+}$ (from water) alongside the solute's metal ion. For a reactive metal such as sodium, $\mathrm{H^+}$ is discharged in preference to the metal ion, so hydrogen gas, not the metal, forms at the cathode; only for a metal less reactive than hydrogen does the metal itself form.
misconceptions.remediation: Before predicting any aqueous cathode product, write down both candidate cations present (the metal ion and $\mathrm{H^+}$ from water) and only then decide which one is actually discharged, rather than assuming the named solute's ion automatically wins.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: A molten ionic compound still contains water, so $\mathrm{H^+}$ and $\mathrm{OH^-}$ from water can also be discharged in the molten case, just as in the aqueous case.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: Learners meet the aqueous case and the molten case close together and blend the two rule-sets, forgetting that 'molten' specifically means the pure solid compound heated until it liquefies, with no water added at all.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner mentions hydrogen or oxygen from water when explaining the electrolysis of molten lead(II) bromide.
misconceptions.correct_model: A molten ionic compound is the pure compound itself, liquefied by heat; no water is present, so the only ions available for discharge are the compound's own ions, for example only $\mathrm{Pb^{2+}}$ and $\mathrm{Br^-}$ for molten lead(II) bromide.
misconceptions.remediation: Before predicting products, ask explicitly 'is water present in this electrolyte, yes or no?'; for molten compounds the answer is always no, which immediately rules out any water-derived product.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: Hydrogen gas forms at the anode, because hydrogen is a gas and gases are assumed to collect at the anode.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: Learners notice that gases are produced at both electrodes in several of these reactions and link 'being a gas' to a fixed electrode, rather than tracking the actual charge on the particle being discharged.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner places hydrogen gas at the anode when predicting the products of dilute sulfuric acid or concentrated sodium chloride solution.
misconceptions.correct_model: Which electrode a product forms at depends only on the charge of the ion discharged there, never on whether the product happens to be a gas. $\mathrm{H^+}$ is a positive ion, so it migrates to the cathode and hydrogen gas is always produced at the cathode, whether or not other gases also form at the anode in the same cell.
misconceptions.remediation: Always name the ion before naming the product: identify that hydrogen gas comes specifically from $\mathrm{H^+}$, a cation, and cations are discharged only at the cathode, regardless of the product's physical state.

common_mistakes.mistake: Predicting the solute's own metal at the cathode for any aqueous electrolysis.
common_mistakes.why: The molten case (only one cation available) is over-generalised to the aqueous case, where water adds a competing cation.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Always name both candidate cations at the cathode (the metal ion and $\mathrm{H^+}$) and compare the metal's reactivity to hydrogen before deciding.

common_mistakes.mistake: Allowing hydrogen or oxygen as possible products of a molten electrolyte.
common_mistakes.why: The aqueous and molten rule-sets are learned close together and blur into one.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Ask explicitly whether water is present before predicting any product; a molten compound never contains water.

common_mistakes.mistake: Placing a gas at an electrode based on it 'being a gas' rather than the charge of the ion producing it.
common_mistakes.why: Several of these cells produce a gas at both electrodes, which hides that each gas's electrode is set by its ion's charge.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Name the ion first (and its charge sign), then decide the electrode from that charge, only naming the product last.

exam_notes: Always name both candidate ions at an electrode before choosing the product; an answer that jumps straight to the product without naming the competition rarely earns full marks.
State explicitly whether water is present in the electrolyte as the first step in any product-prediction answer; this single sentence pre-empts several common errors.
Give an observation (colour, state, test result) alongside every named product where the question allows it; naming without evidence is often only partial credit.

summary.big_idea: The product at each electrode is whichever ion actually wins the competition to be discharged there; water, when present, adds extra competing candidates that a molten compound never has.
key_points: A molten binary compound has only its own two ions present: metal at the cathode, non-metal at the anode, always.
In aqueous solution, $\mathrm{H^+}$ competes with the solute's metal ion at the cathode; hydrogen wins unless the metal is less reactive than hydrogen.
At the anode, a concentrated halide ion is discharged in preference to water; with no halide present, water is oxidised to oxygen instead.
Which electrode a product appears at is decided by the charge of the ion discharged, never by the product's physical state.
summary.what_to_remember_if_nothing_else: Before naming any product, ask: is water present, and if so, which candidate ion actually wins at each electrode?

exit_check.question: Molten calcium bromide, $\mathrm{CaBr_{2}}$, and dilute hydrobromic acid, $\mathrm{HBr(aq)}$, are each electrolysed with inert electrodes. Predict the cathode product for each, and explain why they differ.
exit_check.answer: Molten $\mathrm{CaBr_{2}}$: calcium metal at the cathode ($\mathrm{Ca^{2+} + 2e^- \rightarrow Ca}$), since only $\mathrm{Ca^{2+}}$ and $\mathrm{Br^-}$ are present. Dilute $\mathrm{HBr(aq)}$: hydrogen gas at the cathode ($\mathrm{2H^+ + 2e^- \rightarrow H_{2}}$), since its only cation is $\mathrm{H^+}$ itself. They differ because the molten compound supplies a metal cation with no water to compete, while the aqueous acid has no metal ion at all, only $\mathrm{H^+}$.

03_Charge_transfer_and_copper_electrodes.title: Charge transfer and copper electrodes
03_Charge_transfer_and_copper_electrodes.subject: Chemistry

objectives.statement: Trace the electron path in the external circuit and the ion paths in the electrolyte for the electrolysis of copper(II) sulfate solution, and explain how the result differs between inert (graphite) electrodes and copper electrodes.
Construct a balanced cathode reduction half-equation for a given ion, checking that both atoms and charge balance on the two sides.

prerequisites.statement: an earlier lesson: an ion reaching an electrode is discharged there, gaining or losing electrons to become a neutral atom or molecule; $\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}$ is discharged at a cathode to form copper metal.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: This lesson builds a formal half-equation out of exactly that discharge idea, and compares what happens when the electrode material itself can also react.

prerequisites.statement: C02: the charge on a simple ion, and that a neutral atom has overall charge zero.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Balancing a half-equation by charge requires adding up ion charges and electron charges correctly on each side.

diagnostic_items.question: A copper(II) ion is written Cu2+. How many electrons must it gain to become a neutral copper atom, and what is the overall charge once it has gained them?
diagnostic_items.expected_answer: It must gain 2 electrons. Each electron carries a charge of 1-, so starting from 2+ and adding two lots of 1- gives an overall charge of 0, which is what a neutral copper atom must have.

common_wrong_answers.answer: One electron, because the 2 in Cu2+ tells you there are two copper atoms.
common_wrong_answers.interpretation: The learner is reading the 2 as a count of atoms, as in a formula such as H2, instead of as the size of the charge.

common_wrong_answers.answer: It must lose 2 electrons to become neutral.
common_wrong_answers.interpretation: The learner has the direction of electron transfer reversed: losing electrons makes an ion more positive, so only gaining them can bring 2+ down to 0.

diagnostic_items.interpretation: Every cathode half-equation in this lesson is built by turning an ion's charge into a number of electrons. A learner who cannot do that step cannot write or check a half-equation, whatever they remember about copper.
diagnostic_items.remediation_action: Ask the learner to count along a number line: start at +2, add one electron to reach +1, add a second to reach 0. Then repeat for Ag+ (one electron) and Al3+ (three electrons) so the rule 'the charge tells you how many' is seen to generalise.

theory_blocks.title: Where does the cathode's electron actually come from?
theory_blocks.body:
A $\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}$ ion arrives at the cathode and needs two electrons to become a neutral copper atom.

It is tempting to think of this as the cathode simply 'having' electrons available, but every one of those electrons has a specific origin: it was pushed out of the power supply's negative terminal, travelled along the wire, and arrived at the cathode at the same moment the ion did.

Nothing is created from nothing. At the very same time, at the anode, some other particle is being oxidised, releasing an electron into the wire on the other side, which is what lets the supply keep pushing electrons around at all.

[[blue:The cathode reaction and the anode reaction are not independent events]]; they are locked together by the same flow of electrons through the one external circuit.

theory_blocks.title: Writing and checking a cathode half-equation
theory_blocks.body:
A **half-equation** shows what happens to one ion at one electrode, including the electrons involved. For $\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}$ discharged at the cathode: $$\mathrm{Cu^{2+} + 2e^- \rightarrow Cu}$$

Check it twice, separately:

- **Atoms:** one copper atom on the left (as the ion), one copper atom on the right. Balanced.
- **Charge:** on the left, $(+2) + 2\times(-1) = 0$; on the right, neutral $\mathrm{Cu}$ has charge $0$. Balanced.

Both checks must pass. A half-equation that balances atoms but not charge, or charge but not atoms, is not finished.

theory_blocks.title: Copper(II) sulfate solution with inert (graphite) electrodes
theory_blocks.body:
At the cathode, the candidate cations are $\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}$ and $\mathrm{H^+}$ (from water);

copper is less reactive than hydrogen, so $\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}$ wins and is discharged, depositing copper metal, seen as a pink-brown coating on the cathode: $\mathrm{Cu^{2+} + 2e^- \rightarrow Cu}$.

At the anode, the candidate anions are $\mathrm{SO_{4}^{2-}}$ and $\mathrm{OH^-}$/water; sulfate is not discharged under these conditions (it is left behind in solution), so water is oxidised, giving oxygen, seen as bubbles of colourless gas that relight a glowing splint: $\mathrm{2H_{2}O \rightarrow O_{2} + 4H^+ + 4e^-}$.

Because graphite is inert, this is the only process available at the anode; the electrode itself does not react and keeps its mass and shape unchanged.

Because $\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}$ ions are removed from the solution and not replaced, the blue colour of the solution gradually fades.

assets.caption: Two cells compared: copper(II) sulfate solution with graphite electrodes (left) and with copper electrodes (right). In both, the d.c. supply drives $\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}$ to the cathode, where it is reduced to copper metal, while $\mathrm{SO_{4}^{2-}}$ migrates to the anode without being discharged. With graphite, the anode is unchanged and oxygen bubbles off; with copper, the anode itself dissolves as $\mathrm{Cu \rightarrow Cu^{2+} + 2e^-}$, so the cathode's gain in mass is matched by the anode's loss in mass. The half-equation for each electrode is written under its cell.
assets.purpose: A paired apparatus diagram with explicit ion-migration arrows that lets a learner see directly why the electrode material changes the anode product, pre-empting the related idea.

theory_blocks.title: Copper(II) sulfate solution with copper electrodes
theory_blocks.body:
Swap the graphite anode for a copper anode, everything else unchanged. The cathode half-equation is identical: $\mathrm{Cu^{2+} + 2e^- \rightarrow Cu}$, copper still deposits there. At the anode, copper atoms from the electrode itself are oxidised in preference to water, because copper is oxidised more readily than water under these conditions: $$\mathrm{Cu \rightarrow Cu^{2+} + 2e^-}$$

No gas forms at this anode; instead, the copper anode slowly dissolves (it becomes thinner and loses mass) while pink-brown copper builds up on the cathode, releasing $\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}$ ions back into the solution.

Because the cathode half-equation consumes electrons at the same rate the anode half-equation releases them (both use 2 electrons per copper atom),

the mass gained at the cathode exactly matches the mass lost at the anode, and the concentration of $\mathrm{CuSO_{4}}$ in the solution, and so its blue colour,

stays constant over time: copper is simply transferred from the anode to the cathode, atom for atom.

theory_blocks.title: Active versus inert: one question decides it
theory_blocks.body:
The single question that separates an **inert** electrode (graphite, platinum) from an **active** electrode (such as copper here) is: [[blue:can the electrode material itself be more easily oxidised than anything else available at that electrode?]] For graphite, the answer is always no, so only the electrolyte's ions and water can react.

For a copper anode in a solution already containing $\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}$, the answer is yes, so the electrode dissolves instead of a gas forming.

This is not a special exception to the discharge rules from the previous lesson; it is simply one more candidate (the electrode material itself) added to the competition at that one electrode.
