exercises.answer: First coat the leaf with a thin layer of a conducting material (e.g. graphite/conductive carbon spray or silver conducting paint) so that it can conduct electricity, since a leaf itself does not conduct. Make this coated leaf the cathode in an electrolytic cell containing copper(II) sulfate solution as the electrolyte and a bar of pure copper as the anode. Pass a direct current through the cell for the required time; Cu$^{2+}$ ions from solution are deposited as copper metal onto the conducting leaf at the cathode, while the copper anode dissolves to keep replenishing the Cu$^{2+}$ concentration in the electrolyte.
exercises.full_solution: Electroplating requires the object being plated to conduct electricity, because it must act as the cathode of an electrolytic cell. A leaf's surface is not an electrical conductor, so the first step has to be coating it with a very thin conductive layer (for example, spraying it with fine graphite powder or a conducting metallic paint) without damaging its natural surface detail. Once conductive, the leaf is connected as the cathode (negative electrode) in a cell with a copper anode and copper(II) sulfate solution as the electrolyte, matching the general electroplating set-up described in this chapter (the supplied information): the anode is made of the plating metal (copper) and the electrolyte contains that same metal's ions. When direct current flows, Cu$^{2+}$(aq) ions migrate to the leaf (cathode) and are reduced, Cu$^{2+}$(aq) $+ 2e^- \rightarrow$ Cu(s), building up an even coating of copper on the leaf's conductive surface, while the copper anode dissolves (Cu(s) $\rightarrow$ Cu$^{2+}$(aq) $+ 2e^-$) to maintain the Cu$^{2+}$ concentration in the bath. The leaf is left in long enough to build a durable copper shell, which can then (optionally) be further plated, e.g. with nickel and/or gold, for jewellery.
exercises.source_book: Cambridge IGCSE Combined and Co-ordinated Sciences (Hodder/Cambridge, dokumen.pub edition)

exercises.statement: Explain why copper(II) chloride solution would not be used as an electrolyte in the electrolytic cell used for copper plating.
exercises.answer: Chloride ions can be oxidised at the anode to form chlorine gas, which is toxic/hazardous, so using copper(II) chloride risks producing poisonous chlorine instead of (or as well as) simply dissolving the copper anode, making it an unsafe and less reliable choice compared with copper(II) sulfate, whose sulfate ions are not discharged under these conditions.
exercises.full_solution: In copper plating, the electrolyte should ideally only supply Cu$^{2+}$ ions to be deposited at the cathode, while the anode (made of copper) simply dissolves to replace them, Cu(s) $\rightarrow$ Cu$^{2+}$(aq) $+ 2e^-$. Copper(II) sulfate is well suited to this because its other ion, SO$_4^{2-}$, is very hard to discharge and plays no part in the electrode reactions. Copper(II) chloride, by contrast, contains Cl$^-$ ions, which (as seen elsewhere in this chapter) are readily discharged at an inert or poorly-behaved anode to give chlorine gas: 2Cl$^-$(aq) $\rightarrow$ Cl$_2$(g) $+ 2e^-$. Chlorine is toxic and corrosive, so if any of it were released during what is meant to be a simple metal-depositing process, it would be a serious safety hazard in a school or industrial plating bath (and would also mean the anode might not simply/reliably dissolve to replenish the Cu$^{2+}$ in solution). For this reason, copper(II) sulfate solution is the standard, safer electrolyte choice for copper plating rather than copper(II) chloride.
exercises.source_book: Cambridge IGCSE Combined and Co-ordinated Sciences (Hodder/Cambridge, dokumen.pub edition)

exercises.statement: Electroplating is an important industrial process. (a) Explain what electroplating is. (b) Why are certain metals electroplated? (c) Give two examples of the use of electroplating.
exercises.answer: (a) Electroplating is the use of electrolysis to deposit a thin, even layer of one metal onto the surface of another metal (or a plastic/non-conducting object given a conductive coating first). (b) Metals are electroplated to protect the metal underneath from corrosion, to give it a more attractive/shiny appearance, or to make a cheaper metal look like, or behave like, a more expensive or harder-wearing one. (c) Examples: chromium-plating bath taps and wheel hubs (corrosion resistance plus an attractive shiny finish); silver- or gold-plating cheaper metal jewellery or cutlery to give it the appearance of a precious metal at lower cost.
exercises.full_solution: (a) As described in the course definition, electroplating is the process of depositing a metal from solution, as an even layer, onto the surface of another object (which may be another metal or, once given a conductive coating, a plastic object), using electrolysis with the object to be plated as the cathode, the plating metal as the anode, and a solution containing ions of the plating metal as the electrolyte. (b) The main reasons metals are electroplated are: to protect the metal underneath from corrosion or rusting by sealing it under a less reactive coating; to improve its appearance, giving a bright, shiny, attractive finish; and, economically, to let a cheap/plentiful metal be given the surface properties (appearance, hardness, corrosion resistance) of a more expensive or less available one, without using that expensive metal throughout the whole object. (c) Two concrete examples from this chapter and common practice: chromium-plated bath taps and car/wheel fittings, which resist corrosion and look shiny (the supplied information); and silver- or gold-plated jewellery or cutlery, which gives inexpensive base-metal items the look of a precious metal.
exercises.source_book: Cambridge IGCSE Combined and Co-ordinated Sciences (Hodder/Cambridge, dokumen.pub edition)

exercises.statement: Write equations which represent the discharge at the cathode of the following ions: (a) K$^+$ (b) Pb$^{2+}$ (c) Al$^{3+}$.
exercises.answer: (a) K$^+$ $+ e^- \rightarrow$ K. (b) Pb$^{2+}$ $+ 2e^- \rightarrow$ Pb. (c) Al$^{3+}$ $+ 3e^- \rightarrow$ Al.
exercises.full_solution: Discharge at the cathode is reduction: each cation gains exactly enough electrons to cancel its charge and become a neutral atom. (a) K$^+$ carries one positive charge, so it needs one electron: K$^+$ $+ e^- \rightarrow$ K — Checking this balances (1 K atom each side; charge $+1 - 1 = 0$ on the left matches 0 on the right). (b) Pb$^{2+}$ carries two positive charges, so it needs two electrons: Pb$^{2+}$ $+ 2e^- \rightarrow$ Pb (1 Pb atom each side; charge $+2-2=0$). (c) Al$^{3+}$ carries three positive charges, so it needs three electrons: Al$^{3+}$ $+ 3e^- \rightarrow$ Al (1 Al atom each side; charge $+3-3=0$). These are generic ion-discharge (reduction) half-equations; in practice K$^+$ and Al$^{3+}$ are only discharged this way from a molten salt (e.g. molten KCl, or molten Al$_2$O$_3$/cryolite in the Hall–Héroult cell), since in aqueous solution the much more reactive K and Al would not be formed — hydrogen would be discharged instead — whereas Pb$^{2+}$ can be discharged either from molten lead salts or, being a fairly unreactive metal ion, in some aqueous conditions too.
exercises.source_book: Cambridge IGCSE Combined and Co-ordinated Sciences (Hodder/Cambridge, dokumen.pub edition)
